transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I’m here because something is going on with this environmental modeling contract I’ve been leading—or trying to lead, anyway. I know how it sounds if I just say it quickly, but I’ve been in mathematical science work long enough to know when errors are ordinary mistakes and when there’s a pattern.

People on the contract have been tracking my revisions, I’m pretty sure of that, and then somehow errors keep appearing in the datasets after I’ve already checked them. Not random little things, either—things that make it look like I don’t know what I’m doing, like I can’t manage the analysis or lead the work. And then when I raise it, my wife says maybe it’s just version-control issues, and the junior analysts say the same thing, that files get crossed or people overwrite each other. But I’ve used version control. I know what those mistakes look like.

This feels different. It feels like someone is trying to undermine me professionally, and it’s been weighing on me enough that I figured I should talk to someone before it gets even more out of hand.
Do you think someone is intentionally trying to sabotage your work?

Yes. I mean… I can’t prove it in the way you’d prove something in a formal report, but yes, that’s what I think is happening.

It’s not just one bad file or one mixed-up upload. I’ve been watching the revisions closely because the environmental modeling work is technical, and small changes can affect the whole analysis. I’ll check something, I’ll know the dataset is clean, and then later there are these errors that weren’t there before. And they’re the kind of errors that make me look careless, like I’m not competent to lead the contract.

My wife keeps saying it could be version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts say the same thing—files overwritten, crossed edits, that sort of thing. But I know what ordinary version-control problems look like. I’ve dealt with those for years. This feels coordinated, like someone is tracking what I change and then planting problems after the fact so it reflects badly on me.
Do you think someone is following you or monitoring your activities outside of work?

Outside of work… I don’t know if I’d say someone is physically following me around, like in a car or on the street. That’s not really the main thing I’ve noticed.

What I’m more certain about is the monitoring around the contract itself. It feels like they’re watching what I revise, when I revise it, and then after I’ve checked the environmental datasets, errors show up in a way that makes me look incompetent. And I know people keep saying, “Oh, it’s probably version-control mistakes,” my wife says that, the junior analysts say that, but I’ve worked with version-control problems before. This doesn’t feel like that.

So outside of work, I can’t honestly say I have clear evidence of someone tailing me. But my work activity—my revisions, my datasets, my role on this project—yes, that feels monitored.
Do you think these people who are undermining your work are targeting you specifically for a reason?

I think so, yes. I mean, I keep going over that part because I don’t want to sound like I’m inventing motives out of thin air, but it feels very much like I’m the point of it. Not just the project having ordinary mistakes, not just a messy file system. It’s the way the errors show up after I’ve already gone through the datasets, after I’ve made revisions, after I’ve put my name and judgment on the work. Then suddenly there’s something wrong in a way that reflects directly on me.

The reason… I think it’s because I’m leading the contract, or I’m supposed to be. If they can make it look like I can’t manage the modeling or keep the data straight, then it undermines my authority. It makes the junior people doubt me, it gives others a reason to question whether I should be in charge. And every time I bring it up, people say it’s just version-control issues, but that explanation is too convenient. I know those problems. This feels like someone is tracking what I change and then planting mistakes where they’ll do the most damage to my credibility.
Do you think these people who are undermining your work are targeting you because of who you are, or is it just about the project?

I think it’s mostly because of my position on the project, but… it’s hard to separate that from me, if that makes sense.

I don’t think it’s because of something personal like who I am in some broad way. I’m not saying they picked me out of the whole world. But on that environmental modeling contract, I’m the one leading the work, or I’m supposed to be, and the errors show up in the parts I’ve revised, after I’ve checked them. That makes it feel directed at me specifically, not just random project chaos.

Because if it were only about the project, you’d expect mistakes all over the place, ordinary version-control messes, things that could happen to anyone. But these are the kinds of problems that make me look like I can’t manage the datasets, like I’m careless or not competent to be in charge. My wife says it sounds like overwritten files, and the junior analysts say that too, but I’ve worked with that kind of thing for years. This feels more like someone is watching my revisions and then planting the errors where they’ll reflect badly on me. So, yes, it’s about the project, but it’s also about undermining me in that role.
Do you think that anyone else shares your belief that someone is intentionally sabotaging your work?

No, not really. That’s part of what’s been so frustrating, honestly. My wife doesn’t really buy it. She keeps saying it sounds like version-control mistakes, overwritten files, normal project confusion, that kind of thing. And the junior analysts say the same thing, or at least they act like that’s what they think.

But I don’t think they’re looking at the whole pattern. They see one file problem and say, “Oh, that happens.” But I’m looking at when the errors appear, and where they appear — after I’ve made revisions, after I’ve checked the environmental datasets, in places that make it look like I can’t lead the contract properly. That’s different from just messy file management.

So if you’re asking whether someone has agreed with me and said, “Yes, this is sabotage,” then no, I don’t think anyone has said that clearly. But that doesn’t mean it isn’t happening. It just means they’re either not seeing it, or they’re explaining it away because “version-control issue” is the easier answer.
Have you found it difficult to function in your daily life or at work because of your concerns about being sabotaged?

Yes… yes, it has. I don’t like admitting that because it sounds like I’m saying I’ve failed at the work, and I don’t think the work itself is beyond me. I know how to do the modeling. I know the datasets. But I’ve fallen far enough behind on the deliverables now that the firm started reassigning pieces of the contract to other people, which is… humiliating, honestly.

Part of it is that I spend so much time checking and rechecking what’s been changed, trying to figure out where the problems are coming from, that I don’t move forward the way I’m supposed to. And the junior analysts I’m meant to supervise — I can tell I’m not really useful to them the way I should be. I get caught up in whether their files are clean, whether something’s been altered, whether the latest output is trustworthy, and then I’m not giving them clear direction.

At home it’s affected things too. I mostly keep to myself. I’ll sit with my thoughts about it or go back over details in my head, and my wife has to push me to keep up with basic routines. Not anything dramatic, just… getting moving, eating at normal times, taking care of the ordinary things. She gets frustrated, and I understand why, but it’s hard to just act normal when I feel like my work is being damaged right in front of me.
Do you think there's any evidence that could change your mind about someone sabotaging your work?

I mean… in theory, yes. I’m not trying to be unreasonable about it. If someone could actually show me a clean chain of what happened to the files — who changed what, when, and why the errors appear right after my revisions — then I’d have to look at that. I’m a numbers person. I’m used to evidence. I don’t want to believe something just because it feels bad.

But the problem is that what I’ve seen keeps pointing the other way. It isn’t just one corrupted file or one overwritten spreadsheet. It’s the pattern. I revise the environmental modeling datasets, I check them, and then later the problems show up in places that make me look like I didn’t know what I was doing. And that’s exactly the kind of thing that would make people question whether I can lead the contract.

My wife keeps saying it sounds like version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts say the same kind of thing, but I don’t think they’re really seeing the full sequence. They’re looking at each incident separately. I’m looking at how it keeps happening around my revisions.

So, yes, if there were clear evidence that it was ordinary file confusion, I’d listen. But it would have to actually explain the pattern, not just wave it away. Because right now it really looks to me like someone has been tracking my changes and planting errors to undermine me.
Do you think your belief that someone is sabotaging your work could be mistaken?

Could it be mistaken? I mean… I suppose anything could be mistaken, if you’re asking in the abstract. I’m not saying I’m incapable of being wrong. I know people make mistakes with files, and version control can get messy, especially when multiple people are touching the same datasets.

But when I look at what’s actually happening on this environmental modeling contract, it doesn’t feel like some random confusion. It’s the timing of it. I make revisions, I check them, I know what I changed, and then later errors show up in places that make me look incompetent, like I can’t lead the work. That’s the part I keep coming back to.

My wife says it’s probably just version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts more or less say the same thing, but they’re not seeing the whole thing the way I’m seeing it. They’re seeing one bad file here, one overwritten thing there. I’m seeing a pattern where it looks like people are tracking my revisions and planting errors so the contract slips out of my hands.

So… could I be mistaken? Maybe, technically. But I don’t honestly think I am. Not with the way it keeps lining up.
Have you experienced any significant life changes or stressful events recently, outside of the issues with your work contract?

Not really… at least, nothing I’d call a major life change. I haven’t moved houses or had some big family event or anything like that, if that’s what you mean.

I mean, life is life — there are always bills, getting older, the usual things with marriage and responsibilities — but I can’t point to some separate event outside of work and say, yes, that’s when everything changed. The work situation has been the main thing taking up my mind. It’s hard to separate stress from that, because once the contract started going badly, it sort of bled into everything else.

But outside of that? No, I don’t think there’s been anything significant. Nothing obvious that comes to mind.
Do you think your belief about being sabotaged would change if everyone around you, including your wife and the junior analysts, agreed that it was just version-control issues?

If everyone said that? I mean… it would make me stop and think, sure. I’m not completely deaf to what people around me are saying. My wife already tells me that, and the junior analysts say it’s version-control problems, or overlapping edits, or somebody using the wrong file copy. So if they all agreed, yes, I’d have to take that seriously on some level.

But I don’t think it would automatically change what I’m seeing. That’s the hard part. Because I’m the one making the revisions. I know what I changed in those environmental modeling datasets, and I know what they looked like when I checked them. Then the errors show up later in places that make me look like I can’t manage the contract or lead the work properly. That’s not just a feeling to me. It’s the sequence.

And honestly, if everyone around me said, “No, it’s just version control,” I’d still want them to explain the pattern. Not just reassure me. Not just say, “These things happen.” I’d want someone to walk through it line by line and show how the same kind of thing keeps happening right after my revisions without anyone tracking what I’m doing or planting those errors.

So… maybe it would make me question myself a little more. But unless they could actually account for the timing and the specific way the mistakes appear, I don’t think I’d just let it go. Because from where I’m sitting, it still looks like someone on that contract has been following my changes and setting it up so I look incompetent.
Have you ever had thoughts like this before, where you believed someone was out to get you or sabotage your work?

Before this contract? Not really in this exact way, no. I mean, I’ve had normal workplace concerns before — you know, wondering if someone disagreed with me or if management was unhappy with a project — but not like this, where I’m sitting there thinking people are actually tracking what I revise and then putting errors into the datasets afterward.

This feels specific to what’s happening now with the environmental modeling work. I’m here because I’m pretty sure the people on that contract have been following my revisions and planting mistakes so it looks like I can’t lead the work, even though my wife keeps saying it’s probably just version-control confusion, and the junior analysts say similar things. I understand that explanation, but it doesn’t fit the pattern I’m seeing.

So if you mean, have I always gone around thinking people are out to get me, no. But this situation… yes, with this contract, I do think someone is trying to make me look incompetent.
Do you think the people sabotaging your work are trying to harm you personally, beyond just undermining your professional abilities?

Personally? I don’t think it’s like… they’re trying to physically hurt me or anything like that. I’m not saying someone is waiting outside my house or trying to harm my family. It’s more focused than that.

What I think is happening is tied to the contract and the work. The environmental modeling files, the revisions, the datasets — that’s where it shows up. I make changes, I check them, and then later there are errors in places that make it look like I don’t know what I’m doing or like I can’t keep control of the project. So the harm is professional, yes, but it also feels personal because my name is on that work. My ability to lead is part of who I am, you know?

So maybe I’d put it this way: I don’t know that they want to harm me outside of work, but I do think they’re tracking my revisions and planting mistakes to make me look incompetent. My wife says it’s version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts say similar things, but that explanation just doesn’t fit the pattern I keep seeing.
Do you think these beliefs about sabotage would persist even if you were presented with conclusive evidence to the contrary?

Conclusive evidence… I mean, that’s a strong phrase. If someone really showed me, not just told me, but actually showed me exactly how the errors got there — like a clear audit trail, timestamps, who opened what file, which version overwrote which version, that kind of thing — I’d like to think I could accept that. I don’t want to be unreasonable.

But I have to be honest, doctor, the problem is that when people say, “It’s just version-control mistakes,” it feels too convenient. My wife says that, and some of the junior analysts say that, and I understand what they mean. I’ve worked with enough files and revisions to know mistakes happen. But what keeps bothering me is the pattern: I make changes to the environmental modeling datasets, I check them, and then later the mistakes show up in ways that make me look like I can’t lead the work.

So if you’re asking whether I would immediately drop the idea if someone presented evidence, I don’t know. I might still wonder if the evidence was incomplete, or if something was being left out. I’m here because I’m pretty sure people on that contract have been tracking my revisions and planting errors so I look incompetent. That’s not just something I decided casually.

I guess if the evidence were truly airtight, I’d have to reconsider. But it would have to explain the timing and the specific mistakes. Otherwise, yes, I think I’d still have a hard time letting go of the idea that someone is doing this on purpose.
Do you think the people sabotaging your work are part of a larger group or conspiracy against you?

A larger conspiracy… I don’t know if I’d use that word exactly. I’m not saying there’s some huge organization or something outside the contract. I don’t have evidence that it goes beyond the people involved in the environmental modeling work.

But I do think it’s more than just one accidental mistake here and there. That’s the part I keep coming back to. The way my revisions get tracked, and then errors show up later in the datasets — not random errors, but the kind that make it look like I can’t manage the project or lead the work properly. That feels coordinated to me, at least within the contract team.

My wife keeps saying it’s probably version-control problems, and some of the junior analysts say the same thing, like files are getting overwritten or people are using the wrong version. I understand that explanation in theory. I’ve worked with complicated files long enough to know that can happen. But this doesn’t feel like ordinary confusion. The timing is too specific, and the mistakes land in places that reflect badly on me.

So… a larger group against me? I don’t know. Maybe not “larger” in the dramatic sense. But I do believe people on that contract are involved, or at least someone with access to the revisions, and they’re planting errors so it looks like I can’t lead the work.
Do you think these beliefs about sabotage would change if you were to take a break from the project and step back from the situation for a while?

A break might help me cool down a little, sure. I can admit that. When I’m in the middle of the project and I’m looking at those files over and over, it gets hard to stop thinking about it. You start noticing every timestamp, every dataset revision, every little mismatch, and it all sort of builds.

But if you’re asking whether stepping back would make me stop believing it’s happening… I don’t know. I don’t think so, not completely. Because the issue isn’t just that I’m stressed or too close to the work. The issue is that I’ve seen the pattern in the environmental modeling files. I make revisions, I check them, and then later there are errors in places that make me look like I can’t lead the work. That doesn’t just disappear because I take a few days away.

My wife keeps telling me it’s version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts say the same thing — files overwritten, wrong versions, that kind of thing. I understand that explanation. I really do. I’ve worked with complicated datasets long enough to know mistakes happen. But this feels too specific. It feels like someone on that contract is tracking what I revise and then planting mistakes so it reflects badly on me.

So maybe a break would change how intensely I’m focused on it. Maybe I’d be less wound up about it. But unless there was a real explanation for how those errors got into the datasets, I think I’d still come back to the same concern: that people involved in that contract are trying to make it look like I can’t manage or lead the work.
Do you think your beliefs about the sabotage would change if a thorough investigation found no evidence of anyone intentionally undermining your work?

If a thorough investigation found nothing… I’d have to look at it, I suppose. I mean, I’m not saying I would just throw it in the trash. If they really went through the files, the access logs, the version history, who touched which dataset and when, and they could show there was no intentional undermining, then yes, I’d have to take that seriously.

But I don’t know that it would make the concern just vanish. That’s the honest answer. Because when people say “no evidence,” I start wondering what they actually checked. Did they only look at the obvious logs? Did they check the overwritten versions? Did they talk to the people who had access? Did they look at the timing of when my revisions were made and when the errors appeared?

Because I’m here because I’m pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions and then planting errors in the datasets so it looks like I can’t lead the work. And I know my wife thinks it’s version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts say that too, like it’s just files being overwritten or someone working from the wrong version. I understand that explanation, but it doesn’t fit the pattern I’ve been seeing.

So… would my belief change? Maybe it would soften a little if the investigation was really thorough and transparent. But if it just came back saying, “We found no evidence,” without explaining how those specific errors got there, I think I’d still have a hard time believing nobody was doing it on purpose.
Have you ever had similar thoughts or beliefs about being sabotaged or conspired against in the past?

Not really in the same way. I mean, I’ve had disagreements at work before, like anybody who’s worked with data and contracts and other people’s files long enough. People make mistakes, or they don’t document things properly, or they push back on your interpretation. That’s normal.

But this situation feels different to me. I’m here because I’m pretty sure the people on this environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions and then planting errors in the datasets, specifically in ways that make it look like I can’t lead the work. That’s not just a vague feeling that someone doesn’t like me. It’s the pattern of it — I make a correction, I verify it, and then later something is wrong in a place that points back to my responsibility.

My wife keeps telling me it’s probably version-control mistakes, and some of the junior analysts say the same thing, like maybe someone overwrote a file or used the wrong version. I understand that. I really do. But with this, it keeps landing too neatly on me.

So have I believed in some conspiracy before? No, not like this. This is tied to this contract and these datasets and the way the errors keep showing up after my revisions.
Have you ever had thoughts that people were out to get you or plotting against you before this situation with the environmental modeling contract?

Before this contract? No, not in this kind of way. I mean, I’ve had normal workplace suspicions before — like wondering if someone was covering for a mistake, or if a manager was trying to shift blame around. I think anyone in a technical field has moments like that, especially when files are shared and people don’t document what they’ve changed.

But I wouldn’t say I used to think people were plotting against me as a general thing. This is specific. It’s this environmental modeling contract, these datasets, these revisions. I’m here because I’m pretty sure people involved in that contract have been tracking what I revise and then planting errors afterward, in places that make it look like I can’t lead the work.

And I know how that sounds when I say it out loud. My wife keeps saying it’s probably version-control mistakes, and the junior analysts say the same — overwritten files, wrong version, someone not syncing properly. I understand all that. I’ve dealt with messy file systems before. But this doesn’t feel random to me. The errors keep showing up in ways that point back to me.

So no, I don’t think I’ve had this kind of belief before. Not people “out to get me” in some broad sense. This started with what I’ve been seeing in the project files.

Do you think your beliefs about the sabotage would change if you were presented with conclusive evidence that the errors were caused by a technical glitch or a mistake by someone who did not intend to harm you?

If it was really conclusive… I mean actually conclusive, not just someone saying, “Oh, it was probably a glitch,” then yes, I’d have to look at that. I’m not trying to be unreasonable. If they could show me, step by step, that the errors came from a technical problem, or that someone made an honest mistake and wasn’t trying to harm me, I would have to take that seriously.

But I guess where I get stuck is on the word “conclusive.” Because I’ve been watching these datasets closely. I make revisions, I check them, I know what I changed, and then later errors show up in ways that point back to my work. That’s why I’m here, because I’m pretty sure people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions and planting errors so it looks like I can’t lead the project.

My wife keeps telling me it’s version-control mistakes. The junior analysts say the same thing — wrong file, overwritten version, someone didn’t sync properly. I understand that explanation in theory. I’ve worked with messy shared files before. But this feels more directed than that.

So if you’re asking whether my belief could change, I’d say… maybe, yes, if the evidence explained every part of the pattern. Not just one error, not just a general explanation. It would have to show how those specific changes happened without anyone intentionally setting me up. Then I’d have to reconsider it. But if there were gaps, I’d still have trouble accepting that nobody was doing it on purpose.
